title: A hundred years asleep
hook: a man passes a ruined town, dies a hundred years, and wakes to see his donkey raised (2:259)
carry: he can revive what is dead

segments.voice: Yesterday: no compulsion, and your line, a handhold you grasp yourself. Today, a man asks a hard question out loud, and is answered with a story he lives through.

A traveler rides his donkey past a town that's been destroyed: roofs fallen in, walls collapsed onto themselves, nobody left. He's carrying some food and something to drink. He stops, looks at the ruins, and says what anyone might say: how could God ever bring this back to life? The text doesn't say whether he asks it in wonder or in doubt. And then, the Qur'an says, he finds out. Today: a hundred years asleep.
screen: `A RUINED TOWN, NOBODY LEFT.` → `HOW COULD THIS EVER LIVE AGAIN?` → `THEN HE FINDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred fifty-nine goes on: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him, and asked: how long have you stayed? He answered: a day, or part of a day. That's how waking feels. No, a hundred years. Look at your food and drink: they haven't spoiled. Look at your donkey. And look at the bones, how We set them together and clothe them with flesh. When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God has power over all things. The Qur'an doesn't name the man or the town. The commentators offer names: some say 'Uzayr, whom some identify with Ezra, and the town Jerusalem after its destruction; others name the prophet Jeremiah, or someone else. The story works without a name. Look at the details it does give. The food is unchanged after a century. The donkey, in one reading, has gone to bones and comes back; other commentators read the bones as the man's own. One thing time didn't touch, one thing it took completely, and in the story both are in God's hands. And look where the story sits. Just before it, Ibrahim tells a king: my Lord gives life and causes death. Just after it, Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are raised, and is shown with four birds. Three stories in a row about the same question. The man's question isn't scolded. It's answered with a demonstration he lives through.
screen: `A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY` · `THE FOOD UNSPOILED, THE DONKEY RAISED` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T NAME HIM` · `THREE STORIES, ONE QUESTION`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something old coming back to life, a tree leafing after winter, a friendship starting again, a skill returning to your hands, and look closely at what was dead and what's stirring now. If you pray, hold it up with the man's last words: I know that God has power over all things.
'Uzayr. The name some commentators give the man who doubted a ruined town could live, was made to die a century, and woke to see his donkey raised. Today's word.
Your line: he can revive what is dead. A ruin isn't the end of the story. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims read 2:258–260 together as three stories about God giving life to the dead, and often recall them when speaking of resurrection and of hope after loss.

chat.says: What did the man in the ruined town learn after his hundred years?
options: I know that God has power over all things: He can revive what is dead.
That he had slept only a day, just as he first guessed.
That his food had spoiled, but his donkey was still alive.
chat.meaning: Shown his unspoiled food and the bones clothed with flesh, the man said: I know that God has power over all things (2:259).

'Uzayr.meaning: a name some commentators give the man; some link him to Ezra

Jeremiah.meaning: a prophet some commentators name instead

Jerusalem.meaning: the town some commentators say he passed, after its destruction

Ibrahim.meaning: Abraham, whose two stories sit on either side

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:258 and 2:260 (Ibrahim and the king; Ibrahim and the four birds)
Tafsir at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on 2:259 (identity of the man and the town)

notes: Identifications ('Uzayr, Jeremiah, others; Jerusalem after its destruction) are from the commentaries; 'Uzayr's identification with Ezra is common but debated. Confirm wording.
The man is described as asking sincerely ('it isn't a sneer'); commentators differ on whether he was a believer or a doubter. Confirm.
The 'one thing time didn't touch, one thing it took' reading is the writer's observation, not attributed to a commentator.
